title: Dynamic equilibrium
body: The state in which forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates, so there is no net observable change and the concentrations or partial pressures of all species stay constant.
ced_evidence: 7.1.A.3 "The equilibrium state is dynamic. The forward and reverse processes continue to occur at equal rates"

title: Examples of reversible processes
body: Reversible processes the CED names as examples.

items.label: Absorption and desorption of a gas
Dissolution and precipitation of a salt

ced_evidence: 7.1.A.1 "Many observable processes are reversible"

title: Graphs showing the approach to equilibrium
body: Concentration, partial pressure, or rate versus time graphs used to show how equilibrium is established.

items.label: Concentration or partial pressure vs. time
items.meaning: Reactant and product curves change, then level off to constant values once equilibrium is reached

items.label: Rate vs. time
items.meaning: Forward rate and reverse rate approach each other and become equal at equilibrium

items.label: Constant region
items.meaning: Flat lines indicate no net change, although both processes continue

ced_evidence: 7.1.A.4 "Graphs of concentration, partial pressure, or rate of reaction versus time"

title: Direction from relative forward and reverse rates
body: Forward rate > reverse rate gives net conversion of reactants to products, reverse rate > forward rate gives net conversion of products to reactants, and equal rates mean equilibrium.
ced_evidence: 7.2.A.1 "An equilibrium state is reached when these rates are equal"

title: Equilibrium expression Kc (and Qc) for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD
caution: Qc has the same form but uses concentrations at any time; Kc = Qc only at equilibrium.
ced_evidence: 7.3.A.1 "the law of mass action indicates that the equilibrium expression for (Kc, Qc)"

title: Equilibrium expression Kp (and Qp) for gas-phase reactions
caution: Check whether a question asks for Kc or Kp and use the matching quantities (concentrations vs. partial pressures).
ced_evidence: 7.3.A.1 "for (Kp, Qp) is"

title: Reaction quotient (Q)
body: Q describes the relative concentrations (or partial pressures) of reaction species at any time and tends toward K, so that Kc = Qc and Kp = Qp at equilibrium.
ced_evidence: 7.3.A.1 "The reaction quotient Qc describes the relative concentrations of reaction species at any time"

title: Leave solids and pure liquids out of K and Q
body: Substances whose concentration or partial pressure is independent of amount, such as solids and pure liquids, do not appear in the reaction quotient or equilibrium expression.
ced_evidence: 7.3.A.2 "does not include substances whose concentrations (or partial pressures) are independent of the amount, such as for solids and pure liquids"

title: Magnitude of K and extent of reaction
body: A very large K means the reaction proceeds essentially to completion (products dominate at equilibrium); a very small K means it barely proceeds (reactants dominate).
ced_evidence: 7.5.A.1 "very large K values and proceed essentially to completion. Others have very small K values and barely proceed at all"

title: K for a reversed reaction
body: K_{\text{reverse}}=\frac{1}{K_{\text{forward}}}
ced_evidence: 7.6.A.1 "When a reaction is reversed, K is inverted."

title: K when coefficients are multiplied by c
body: K_{\text{new}}=K^{\,c}
ced_evidence: 7.6.A.2 "multiplied by a factor c, K is raised to the power c"

title: K for summed reactions
body: K_{\text{overall}}=K_1\times K_2\times\cdots
caution: The same algebraic manipulations apply to Q because K and Q have identical mathematical forms.
ced_evidence: 7.6.A.3 "the K of the resulting overall reaction is the product of the K's"

title: Comparing Q with K to find the direction
body: Q < K: net consumption of reactants and formation of products; Q > K: net consumption of products and formation of reactants; Q = K: dynamic equilibrium with constant proportions.
ced_evidence: 7.7.A.2 "When Q < K, the reaction will proceed with a net consumption of reactants"

title: Particulate model of a reversible reaction
body: A particulate representation showing relative numbers of reactant and product particles before and at equilibrium, consistent with the value of K.

items.label: Before equilibrium
items.meaning: Relative numbers of reactant and product particles initially present

items.label: At equilibrium
items.meaning: Both reactant and product particles present, with fixed relative numbers

items.label: Value of K
items.meaning: Particle ratio at equilibrium, raised to the stoichiometric coefficients, gives K

ced_evidence: 7.8.A.1 "Particulate representations can be used to describe the relative numbers of reactant and product particles present prior to and at equilibrium"

title: Stresses to an equilibrium system (Le Châtelier)
body: Stresses whose effects Le Châtelier's principle is used to predict.

items.label: Addition or removal of a chemical species
items.meaning: System shifts to oppose the change

items.label: Change in temperature
items.meaning: System responds to the temperature change

items.label: Change in volume/pressure of a gas-phase system

ced_evidence: 7.9.A.1 "addition or removal of a chemical species, change in temperature, change in volume/pressure of a gas-phase system, or dilution of a reaction system"

title: Observable effects of a stress
body: Le Châtelier's principle predicts how a stress changes experimentally measurable properties such as pH, temperature, and color of a solution.
ced_evidence: 7.9.A.2 "measurable properties such as pH, temperature, and color of a solution"

title: Which stresses change Q and which change K
body: A disturbance makes Q differ from K and the system shifts to restore Q = K; concentration-type stresses change Q only, while a temperature change changes K itself.
ced_evidence: 7.10.A.2 "changes in concentration, cause a change in Q only. A change in temperature causes a change in K."

title: Ksp expression for dissolution of a salt A_aB_b(s)
caution: The solid salt is not written in the expression; use square brackets and raise each ion's concentration to its coefficient.
ced_evidence: 7.11.A.1 "Ksp, the solubility-product constant"; 7.3.A.2

title: Solubility-product constant (Ksp)
body: Ksp is the equilibrium constant that describes the extent of the reversible dissolution of a salt, and it links Ksp to the salt's molar solubility in a saturated solution in either direction.
ced_evidence: 7.11.A.1 "The dissolution of a salt is a reversible process whose extent can be described by Ksp"; 7.11.A.4

title: Ksp and the solubility rules
body: Ksp values greater than 1 correspond to soluble salts, and Ksp can be used to compare the relative solubility of different substances.
ced_evidence: 7.11.A.3 "Ksp values >1 correspond to soluble salts"

title: Common-ion effect
body: The solubility of a salt is reduced when it is dissolved in a solution that already contains one of the ions present in the salt.
caution: Explain it using Le Châtelier's principle (the added common ion shifts dissolution toward the solid) or calculate it from Ksp, rather than citing a rule of thumb.
ced_evidence: 7.12.A.1 "The solubility of a salt is reduced when it is dissolved into a solution that already contains one of the ions present in the salt"
